name: Losar and the Pemayangtse cham
when: February–March, 1st day of the 1st Tibetan month (lunar); cham dances in the days before
summary: Losar, the Tibetan new year, is celebrated by Sikkim's Bhutia, Lepcha and other Buddhist communities with family gatherings, prayers and visits to monasteries. In the days before it, Pemayangtse near Pelling and other gompas hold cham masked dances to clear away the old year's obstacles.
body: Losar marks the start of the Tibetan lunar year and usually falls in February or early March. In Sikkim, families clean and decorate their homes, prepare special foods and visit monasteries to offer prayers and khadas. Gangtok, Pelling and the monastery towns are busy with families in new clothes, and many shops close for a few days.

Before the new year, monasteries perform cham dances to drive out negative forces of the past year. At Pemayangtse, the annual dance is held on the 28th and 29th days of the twelfth Tibetan month, with monks in masks and robes representing deities and protectors, accompanied by long horns, drums and cymbals. Rumtek and other Gangtok monasteries hold their own dances in the same season.

For travellers, Losar is a chance to see Sikkim's Buddhist traditions at their most public. It is cold in February, especially in Pelling's mornings, but the skies are often clear. Dates shift each year with the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Arrive at Pemayangtse early on dance days to find a place in the courtyard.
Dress warmly; dances run for hours in cold winter air.
Do not use flash and do not walk across the dance area.

faqs.a: Losar falls on the first day of the Tibetan lunar year, usually in February or early March. Dates change each year; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where can I see cham dances before Losar?
faqs.a: Pemayangtse near Pelling, Rumtek and Enchey near Gangtok and other monasteries hold masked dances in the days before Losar.
Yes, monastery dances are open to visitors. Dress modestly, follow instructions on photography and respect the rituals.
Less than in October or May. Some shops and offices close for a few days, so plan meals and travel ahead.

name: Saga Dawa
when: May–June, full moon of the 4th Tibetan month (lunar)
summary: Saga Dawa is the holiest month of the Tibetan Buddhist calendar, honouring the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing. On its full moon, Gangtok holds a procession of monks carrying holy texts through the city, and Buddhists across Sikkim visit monasteries and make offerings.
body: Saga Dawa falls in the fourth month of the Tibetan calendar, and its full moon day, usually in May or June, is the most important. Buddhists believe merit earned during this month is multiplied, so many people give to charity, avoid eating meat and visit monasteries to pray and light butter lamps.

In Gangtok, monks from local monasteries lead a procession through the city carrying holy books, accompanied by horns, drums and devotees. The procession moves through the main streets, and people come out to receive blessings. Monasteries across the state, including Rumtek and those around Ravangla and Pelling, hold prayers and rituals.

For visitors, Saga Dawa coincides with the busy May and early June season and pre-monsoon weather. The procession is a public event; watch from the roadside and avoid blocking the route. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Ask your hotel the date and route of the Gangtok procession in advance.
Watch from a step or roadside rather than joining unless invited.
Carry a light rain jacket; showers are common in late May and June.

faqs.a: On the full moon of the fourth Tibetan month, usually in May or June. The whole month is considered holy. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens on Saga Dawa in Gangtok?
faqs.a: Monks lead a procession through the city carrying holy texts, accompanied by music and devotees. Monasteries hold prayers and butter-lamp offerings.

faqs.q: Can tourists join the Saga Dawa procession?
faqs.a: Visitors can watch from the roadside. Join only if invited, dress modestly and do not block the route.

faqs.q: Is Saga Dawa a public holiday in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Saga Dawa has been a state holiday in Sikkim, so some offices and shops close. Check current status before you travel.

name: Pang Lhabsol
when: August–September, 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month (lunar)
summary: Pang Lhabsol is a festival unique to Sikkim that honours Mount Kangchenjunga as the guardian deity of the land. It also commemorates a traditional blood-brotherhood pact between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples. Masked warrior dances are held at monasteries including Gangtok's palace chapel and Ralang near Ravangla.
body: Pang Lhabsol falls on the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in late August or September. It was developed under the Chogyals and centres on the worship of Kangchenjunga, called Dzö-nga, as the guardian spirit of Sikkim. It also remembers a pact of brotherhood between the Lepcha and Bhutia communities, sealed in tradition at Kabi Longstok near Gangtok.

The most striking part is the masked dance. Monks dressed as warriors and as the guardian deities of Kangchenjunga perform in monastery courtyards with swords and shields, to drums and long horns. Gangtok's Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel, and Ralang monastery near Ravangla are among the main venues.

The festival falls at the end of the monsoon, so rain and road disruptions are still possible. It is a state holiday, and local families attend in traditional dress. Dates follow the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.
tips: Ask locally for the venue and timing of the dances; they vary by year.
Carry rain gear and plan extra travel time in late monsoon weather.
Do not use flash and stay out of the dance area.

faqs.a: A festival unique to Sikkim honouring Mount Kangchenjunga as the guardian deity and commemorating a pact between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples, with masked warrior dances.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh Tibetan month, usually late August or September. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where can I see the Pang Lhabsol dances?
faqs.a: At Tsuklakhang in Gangtok, Ralang monastery near Ravangla and other monasteries. Ask locally for the year's schedule.

faqs.q: Is Pang Lhabsol a good time to visit Sikkim?
faqs.a: It is a rare cultural event, but it falls at the end of the monsoon, so expect some rain and road delays. Keep plans flexible.
